You use Google services every day. If you want to look up something online, you use Google's search engine. If you want to check your email, you will use Gmail to do so. If you want to go to a place, you will (have) to use Google Maps because it's your only option; it has every single place. Even your phone has Android (unless you use an iPhone). This is called an **ecosystem**. All of the Google services you use work together in harmony. It feels convenient. You think it's all free, but you are actually paying the cost by giving away your privacy instead of your money. In this post, I will share some alternatives to help you escape the Google ecosystem. Though some apps are irreplaceable, like Google Maps, shopkeepers and business owners usually only add their places to Google Maps. I will try to help you escape Google's ecosystem, but not all the options I have listed below are "private".

## 1. Google Search &rarr; [DuckDuckGo](https://duckduckgo.com/?ref=lakshyasinghchauhan.com), [Brave Search](https://search.brave.com/?ref=lakshyasinghchauhan.com)
This is by far the most commonly used Google service, and the easiest to replace too. DuckDuckGo is the best alternative to Google Search, and it's actually good too. I even use it myself daily. Though if you don't like the fact that DuckDuckGo uses Bing for its search results, you have Brave Search, a search engine from the creators of the Brave Browser. Its features are also nice, like Goggles, which pulls results from other search engines if you can't find something. Both are genuine choices.

## 2. Gemini &rarr; [Duck.ai](https://duck.ai/?ref=lakshyasinghchauhan.com), [ChatGPT](https://chatgpt.com/?ref=lakshyasinghchauhan.com)
We again have DuckDuckGo, but this time for their LLMs. It uses LLMs such as GPT-6 or Meta's LLMs, but they anonymise your prompts. If you don't care about your privacy, you are free to go to ChatGPT or Claude.

## 3. Google Maps, Waze &rarr; [Apple Maps](https://maps.apple.com/?ref=lakshyasinghchauhan.com), [OpenStreetMap](https://www.openstreetmap.org/?ref=lakshyasinghchauhan.com)
Yes, Waze is owned and operated by Google; that's why they have the same results for places as Google Maps does. Anyways, Apple Maps and OpenStreetMap are the best alternatives here, though they don't have as many places as Google Maps. If you live in India like me, you might already know that nobody uses Apple Maps or other map apps other than Google Maps (or there is a slight chance you can find a Wazer).

## 4. Gmail &rarr; [Proton Mail](https://mail.proton.me/?ref=lakshyasinghchauhan.com)
For this one, I could find only one good alternative: Proton Mail. Yes, it has a premium subscription option too, but it's not required. And besides, Google has a subscription too. If you are wondering what paying for Proton Mail gets you, it gets you more storage and the ability to use Thunderbird or other mail clients like that. The reason I didn't include Outlook was that it's a bit too bloated in my opinion. You can also import all of your mail to Proton Mail directly.

## 5. Google Drive &rarr; [Proton Drive](https://drive.proton.me/?ref=lakshyasinghchauhan.com), [TeraBox](https://terabox.com/?ref=lakshyasinghchauhan.com)
Google Drive is the place where you upload your homework or files you want to share with a group for easy access and editing, and it's replaceable too. If you get Proton Mail, you already get yourself access to the Proton tools suite, which also includes Proton Drive. If you want a lot of storage, you've got TeraBox, which gives you 1TB of storage for free, and it can also import all of your files from Google Drive.

## 6. Google Docs Suite &rarr; [Proton Docs](https://docs.proton.me/?ref=lakshyasinghchauhan.com), [LibreOffice](https://www.libreoffice.org/?ref=lakshyasinghchauhan.com)
For this one, I'd prefer the local options. LibreOffice is an excellent choice when it comes to office editing, and I've even used it for my IT homework. Though if you want cloud options, you've got Proton's Docs suite.

## 7. Google Passwords &rarr; [Bitwarden](https://bitwarden.com/?ref=lakshyasinghchauhan.com), [KeePass](https://keepass.info/?ref=lakshyasinghchauhan.com)
This is also one of those choices where storing your stuff locally is better. Personally, I use KeePassXC as my primary password manager. It's excellent, and supports passkeys, TOTP (authenticator codes), uploading files into your entries, and browser integration. Then, I use Syncthing to sync my passwords between my phone and laptop. On my phone, I use KeePassDX. If you prefer online syncing, you can use Bitwarden. I used Bitwarden for a year before switching to KeePassXC. You can also easily export your passwords from it and import your passwords easily into Bitwarden and KeePassXC.

## 8. Google Chrome &rarr; [Firefox](https://www.firefox.com/?ref=lakshyasinghchauhan.com), [LibreWolf](https://librewolf.net/?ref=lakshyasinghchauhan.com), [Brave](https://brave.com/?ref=lakshyasinghchauhan.com)
Switching browsers might sound difficult and hard to you, but you can easily import your bookmarks and history by just using the import tool in Firefox-based browsers. If you choose to go with Brave, you can just copy your browser profile from Google Chrome and paste it into Brave. The same applies to every other Chromium browser. I am using Firefox because it still supports Manifest V2 extensions, and Brave also does that too.

## 9. Google Blogger &rarr; [WordPress](https://wordpress.org/?ref=lakshyasinghchauhan.com), [Jekyll](https://jekyllrb.com/?ref=lakshyasinghchauhan.com)
Personally, I think Jekyll is the best way to write blogs. It uses Markdown for your posts, meaning that if I ever wanted to switch, I could easily do that. And it also has a community that makes awesome themes, so you don't have to design your own theme. You can, of course, make your own theme easily like I did. Jekyll is a static site generator, and can be hosted for free on GitHub.

## Conclusion
Congratulations on removing Google from your life (for the most part)! If you have any suggestions, leave a comment down below. Thank you for reading!
